Chapter One

Introduction

In open and distance learning (ODL), instructional materials play a vital role in guiding learners through their studies, particularly when they learn independently and across different times and locations. Traditionally, print-based materials have provided the foundation for this process. However, advances in educational technologies have expanded the possibilities for presenting content, facilitating interaction, and supporting learners with diverse learning needs. This calls for a broader approach that moves beyond print to make purposeful use of multiple modes of communication and representation.

Building on the earlier guide, “Bridging the Gap”, which focused primarily on developing print-based instructional materials for ODL at the Open University of Sri Lanka (OUSL), this guide, “Bridging the Gap - Part II: Designing Multimodal Instructional Materials for Open and Distance Learning”, extends the scope to the design and development of multimodal instructional materials for ODL. It explores how written text, visual representations, audio, video, animation, and interactive elements can be purposefully used to enrich content presentation, facilitate learner engagement, and support meaningful learning. It also considers the Moodle learning management system (LMS) and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as tools for developing and adapting content. The guide itself is presented in a multimodal format, using different modes of representation and communication to support the presentation of its content and demonstrate approaches that educators can apply in their own instructional materials. The emphasis is on selecting and integrating different modes according to their pedagogical value, rather than simply using multiple technologies and media formats.

This guide is underpinned by several key principles, including constructive alignment with intended learning outcomes, learner-centredness, purposeful media selection, active learner engagement, accessibility and inclusivity, coherence, and the appropriate use of technology. These principles help educators ensure that different modes complement one another and accommodate ODL learners’ diverse needs. Educators can use this guide either sequentially when developing new instructional materials or refer to specific sections to review and improve the existing materials. The guidance and examples can be adapted to different disciplines, learner characteristics, delivery contexts, and available resources. Ultimately, the guide aims to strengthen educators’ capacity to create accessible, engaging, and pedagogically sound materials that promote learner independence and meaningful achievement in ODL at OUSL.

Chapter Two

Principles and Practices of Open and Distance Learning

Page 1 of 6

Introduction

The principles and practices of ODL are the guidelines and methods that promote flexible, accessible, and effective distance learning.

Before you design instructional materials, you need a clear picture of the system in which they will be used. In this chapter, we will first look at the foundations of ODL: its “open” philosophy, its “distance” reality, and the classical theories that explain it. We will then look at who the ODL learner is. Finally, we will discuss the eight principles that guide ODL and the practices that apply them at the OUSL.

  • Explain the “open” and “distance” dimensions of ODL.
  • Compare the classical theories of distance education put forward by Peters, Holmberg and Moore.
  • Describe the characteristics of the ODL learner.
  • Explain the principles that guide ODL.
  • Identify ODL practices that apply these principles in teaching and learning.

2.1 Foundations of ODL

The two pillars of ODL

ODL is a multi-dimensional approach to education that breaks the traditional mould and is built on two distinct pillars: "Open" philosophy and "Distance" reality. "Openness" refers to the removal of barriers that prevent people from learning, with open entry (minimal or no formal entry requirements), open place (learning happens at home, workplace, or on the move), and open pace (learners decide how fast or slow they want to progress).

Figure 2.1

The "Open" Philosophy - Removing Barriers to Learning

AI-generated image using Gemini.

"Distance", on the other hand, refers to the separation between the teacher and learner in space and/or time. Since the teacher is not physically present to clarify a confusing paragraph or answer a sudden question, the printed material must take over the teacher’s role.

Before designing and developing such material, you must understand the classical theories of distance education that govern ODL. They will help you to tell apart the concept of “distance education” from the theory and practice of correspondence studies, which emerged in the nineteenth century (Fritsch, 2001).

Otto Peters, Börje Holmberg, and Michael Moore are three classical theorists who have been influential in both understanding and practising distance education, and the following table comprehensively presents the respective theories they put forward, their characteristics, and the implementation of their theoretical understanding.

Table 2.1
Characteristic of classical distance education theories
 Otto Peters, (1973)Börje Holmberg (1983)Michael Moore (1993)
TheoryTheory of IndustrialisationGuided Didactic Conversation TheoryTransactional Distance Theory
Main characteristicsDivision of work among cooperating individuals, mechanisation of material production and dissemination, and planning and mass production.· Communication leading to guided didactic conversation.
· Emphasis on one-to-one relationship between tutor and learner in ODL.
· In ODL, responsibility for teaching lies with course designers		· Learning experience is determined by a learning activity.
· Distinct relationship between learner and facilitator in a learning process
· Learner autonomy in shaping their aims, objectives, and assessment and evaluation parameters.
Implementation of theoretical understanding· Distance education as a standardised educational mass system.
· Similar to industrialised production processes.		· Course designed incorporating a conversational tone into the content of the course.
· Dialogue created between learner and teacher, through learning materials.		· Applying appropriate instructional design features to bridge the communication gap between facilitator and learner caused by distance.
· Programme structure, dialogue (i.e., interactions between learning facilitator and learners), and autonomy (i.e., learner’s participation in decision making).

(Source: https://pacificopencourses.col.org)

In a nutshell, the Theory of Industrialisation focuses on treating course production like a high-quality assembly line (writing, editing, printing); the Guided Didactic Conversation Theory, on the idea of text "talking" to the student, using a conversational tone ("Now, try this...") instead of a formal one; and the Transactional Distance Theory, on the learners’ ability to take charge of their own study, providing clear instructions so that they don’t feel lost.

Chapter Two · Page 3 of 6

2.2 The ODL Learner

It is a must that we get to know who an ODL learner is before we cater to him/her with SIMs.

So, who is an ODL learner?

An ODL learner is typically an adult, often juggling work, family, and study. Unlike conventional students, they don't just consume knowledge; they try to fit it into the gaps of their busy life schedules. They are self-directed and prefer to take charge of their own learning journey (Knowles, 1980). Also, they come with years of professional and life experience, which they use to test the validity of what you write in the SIMs. Apart from that, they use these SIMs as a primary connection to the institution, in your case, the OUSL, since most of them are prone to studying in isolation.

The following table will give you a clearer idea of an ODL learner’s profile.

Table 2.2
An ODL learner’s profile at a glance
FeatureDescription
Geographic diversityThey could be studying from a high-rise building in the city or a remote rural village.
Goal orientedThey are usually studying for a specific reason (i.e., career advancement, personal fulfillment).
Limited timeThey study in between their other commitments (i.e., during commutes, after kids are in bed, on lunch breaks)

Being aware of these facts is important to you as ODL academics, as the ODL learner is physically separated from you, and the SIM must act as a "Teacher in Print." It must anticipate their questions, provide the encouragement a tutor would give in person, and bridge the gap between theory and their real-world practice.

Chapter Two · Page 4 of 6

2.3 Principles of ODL

Principles are the fundamental ideas that guide the planning, delivery, and evaluation of ODL.

Figure 2.2

Principles of ODL

Each principle is explained below.

1. Open Access

Opening up learning opportunities by removing barriers related to age, geographical location, social background, and prerequisite entry qualifications.

2. Flexibility

Grant learners the freedom to choose what, when and where to study and at what pace.

3. Learner-Centredness

Empowering learners to take responsibility for their own learning and develop autonomy.

4. Bridging Transactional Distance

Maintaining learner engagement despite physical separation through interactive dialogue between teachers and learners.

5. Equality and Inclusiveness

Designing inclusive learning opportunities that accommodate diverse learner needs through accessible multimedia formats and non-discriminatory practices.

6. Quality and Relevance

Ensuring learning materials, teaching methods, assessments, and learner support meet educational standards and align with learning outcomes.

7. Learner Support and Motivation

Providing academic guidance, technical assistance, feedback, and encouragement to help learners overcome challenges and achieve their learning goals.

8. Lifelong Learning

Encouraging continuous learning and skills development throughout a person's life, regardless of age or educational background.

Chapter Two · Page 6 of 6

Summary and References

Summary

ODL rests on two pillars. The “open” philosophy removes barriers of entry, place and pace. The “distance” reality separates the teacher and the learner, so the learning materials must take over much of the teacher’s role.

Three classical theories explain how this works. Peters described distance education as an industrialised system of course production. Holmberg described learning materials as a guided didactic conversation with the learner. Moore described the transactional distance between teacher and learner, shaped by structure, dialogue and learner autonomy.

The ODL learner is usually an adult who studies around work and family commitments, is goal oriented, and depends on the materials as the main link to the institution.

Eight principles guide ODL: open access, flexibility, learner-centredness, bridging transactional distance, equality and inclusiveness, quality and relevance, learner support and motivation, and lifelong learning. ODL practices, such as SIMs, the LMS, tutor support, flexible assessment and regional centres, put these principles into effect.

In the next chapter, we will look at the modes through which ODL materials reach learners.

References

Fritsch, H. (2001). Distance education. In N. J. Smelser & P. B. Baltes (Eds.), International encyclopedia of the social & behavioral sciences (1st ed., pp. 3781–3784). Pergamon.

Knowles, M. (1980). The modern practice of adult education: From pedagogy to andragogy. https://colllearning.info/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/The-Modern-Practice-of-Adult-Education.pdf

Chapter Three

Modes of ODL Delivery and Multimodal Learning

Page 1 of 6

Introduction

In the earlier guide, “Bridging the Gap”, you learned how print-based Self-Instructional Materials (SIMs) work as a "teacher in print". But today's ODL learners study in many ways: with a printed SIM at home, with a phone on the bus, or in Moodle late at night. One mode alone cannot meet all their needs. This chapter helps you think about how your content reaches learners, and how to choose and combine delivery modes with a clear purpose.

In this chapter, we will first discuss what "mode of delivery" means in ODL and why ODL needs diverse delivery modes. We will then look at six key modes: print-based SIMs, audio, video, the LMS, multimodal materials and OER. Finally, we will discuss how to choose the right mode for your learners and your subject, and how to bring different modes together without overloading learners.

3.1 What does Mode of Delivery mean in ODL?

As an academic in the ODL system, you are not simply delivering content. You are designing learning experiences for students who study at a distance, often on their own and under many constraints.

At the OUSL, print-based self-instructional materials (SIMs) have traditionally been the main mode of delivery. However, with new technology and changing learner needs, ODL delivery has grown beyond a single mode. Today, effective ODL uses a purposeful mix of modes:

Figure 3.1

Modes of delivery in ODL

Before we explore each mode, let’s begin with a brief reflection.

Pause and Reflect

Think about a course you are teaching now.

  • What types of materials do you give your learners?
  • Do you rely mainly on one mode (e.g., printed SIMs)?
  • Have you used any other modes (e.g., videos, LMS activities)?
  • Does your current approach support diverse learner needs?

3.2 Why Do We Need Diverse Delivery Modes?

Now you know what a mode of delivery is, let us see why one mode is not enough. ODL learners differ in access, readiness and learning preferences. A combination of delivery modes helps to:

  • Reach geographically dispersed learners
  • Support diverse learning preferences
  • Improve learner motivation and retention
  • Strengthen "teacher presence" in distance learning (Commonwealth of Learning [COL], 2005)
Figure 3.2

Why ODL needs diverse delivery modes

3 / 6
Chapter Three · Page 4 of 6

3.3 Main Modes of ODL Delivery

Let us now look at each mode one by one. We will start with the mode you know best: print-based SIMs.

3.3.1 Print-Based SIMs

Print-based SIMs are still one of the most reliable modes in ODL. They do not need electricity, internet or special devices, so learners can study anywhere and at any time.

Advantages
  • No need for electricity, internet or devices
  • Learners study at their own pace
  • Easy to go back, re-read and make notes
  • Clear, step-by-step structure
Disadvantages
  • One-way; no instant feedback
  • Slow and costly to update
  • Cannot show sound or movement
  • May limit engagement with complex or abstract ideas

3.3.2 Audio

Audio materials can be a powerful addition to ODL delivery. They let learners hear the teacher's voice, even when they are far away.

Examples: Recorded explanations of difficult concepts · Podcast-style discussions · Audio summaries of lessons

Advantages
  • Learners can listen while travelling or doing daily tasks
  • Supports learners who prefer listening
  • Tone and emphasis can make complex ideas simpler
  • Small files; low data use
Disadvantages
  • Cannot show diagrams, tables or formulas
  • Hard to find one specific point quickly
  • Needs a device to play
  • Learners may lose focus in long recordings

3.3.3 Video

Video allows you to demonstrate processes, visualise abstract ideas and create a sense of teacher presence.

Examples: Short lecture videos · Demonstrations · Screen recordings · Animated explanations

Advantages
  • Shows real processes and skills step by step
  • Makes abstract ideas easier to see
  • Creates a strong sense of teacher presence
  • Learners can pause and replay
Disadvantages
  • Large files; needs good internet or data
  • Takes more time and cost to produce
  • Long, lecture-style videos may overwhelm learners
  • Hard to update once recorded

3.3.4 LMS

So far, we have discussed materials that learners read, hear and watch. Now let us discuss the place where we can bring them together online: the LMS.

The Learning Management System (LMS), such as Moodle, plays a key role in supporting ODL delivery. Through the LMS, you can share extra resources, provide quizzes and self-assessments, facilitate discussions and give feedback.

Examples: Moodle course pages · Online quizzes · Discussion forums · Assignment submission

Advantages
  • All resources in one place
  • Quizzes give instant feedback
  • Supports discussion and interaction
  • Teachers can track progress and give feedback
Disadvantages
  • Needs internet, devices and digital skills
  • Too many links can overload learners
  • Materials uploaded without guidance confuse learners
  • Needs regular updating and moderation

3.3.5 Multimodal Materials

You have now seen each mode on its own. But what happens when we combine them? Let us find out.

Multimodal materials integrate several modes within one learning experience.

Examples: A lesson combining text, visuals, audio and activities · A SIM with links to videos and interactive elements · A digital lesson with embedded quizzes

Advantages
  • Modes support and strengthen each other
  • Suits learners with different preferences
  • Leads to deeper understanding
  • More engaging and interesting
Disadvantages
  • Needs careful planning and more design time
  • Can overload learners if modes are not linked
  • Some parts need devices and internet
  • Needs design skills or team support

Look at Figure 3.3. Can you see the difference between the two designs? Multimodal design is about integration, not just addition.

Figure 3.3

Adding modes versus integrating modes in a multimodal lesson

3.3.6 Open Educational Resources (OER)

You do not always have to create every material yourself. Let us now discuss OER.

OER are freely available learning materials that can be used, adapted and shared.

Examples: Open textbooks · Educational videos · Interactive simulations

Advantages
  • Saves development time
  • Free to use and adapt
  • Provides diverse perspectives
  • Enriches your course materials
Disadvantages
  • May not match your course objectives or local context
  • Quality varies; must check accuracy
  • Licence and attribution rules must be followed
  • May need adapting (language, examples)
Important

Always check that OER are relevant, accurate and aligned with your course objectives, and give proper attribution.

3.4 Choosing the Right Delivery Mode

Now you know the main modes, and their advantages and disadvantages. The next question is: how do you choose the right one?

Choosing a delivery mode is a critical design decision. It should match learner needs, course objectives and institutional capacity. Before you decide, consider these four areas:

Learner profile
  • Access to devices and internet
  • Digital confidence and study skills
  • Language and support needs
Nature of the subject
  • Mainly theory or skills-based?
  • Needs demonstration, practice or reflection?
Available resources
  • Time, cost and production capacity
  • Technical and academic support
Quality and compliance
  • Academic standards and consistency
  • Copyright, licensing and reuse permissions (OUSL, 2016)

Now, let’s watch a short video by Dr. Tony Bates, a well-known expert in online and distance learning. This video will give you a theory-based understanding of how to select the right media and delivery modes for your teaching.

Watch: Dr. Tony Bates on selecting media and delivery modes

Source: YouTube, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-W79hGvukTs

Do you know?

No single delivery mode works for everyone. The most effective ODL programmes use a carefully planned combination of modes, tailored to learners and learning outcomes.

Chapter Four

Developing Print-Based Instructional Materials

Page 1 of 7

Introduction

Are you aware of the foremost service expected of an academic employed in the ODL system? It is designing and developing self instructional materials (SIMs) for their distance learners.

Figure 4.1

An ODL student studying self-instructional materials at a desk

AI-generated image using Gemini.

In the ODL system, SIMs make up the most critical component for delivering education. It is not merely a textbook; it is a meticulously designed learning resource that replaces the physical presence and immediate interaction with the teacher. The core expectation from SIMs is that they must fulfill the multifaceted roles of a traditional classroom teacher.

Let’s first recollect the role of a traditional classroom teacher and that of a SIM.

Table 4.1
Role of a classroom teacher vs role of a SIM
Role of a Classroom TeacherRole of the SIM
Presents content (lecturing)Delivers content (clear, structured explanations)
Guides learning (explaining tasks)Directs the learner (specific learning objectives and activities)
Motivates and engages (enthusiasm, questioning)Fosters engagement (embedded self-assessment questions, reflective tasks)
Provides feedback (checking understanding)Offers immediate feedback (check your progress sections, model answers)
Evaluates performance (tests, assignments)Facilitates self-evaluation (in-between activities, end-of-unit exercises, practice questions)
Creates a friendly atmosphereAdopts a conversational, encouraging tone (uses the pronoun 'you')

Chapter Four · Page 2 of 7

Key Characteristics and Expectations of SIMs

In an ODL context, the material must be designed to be truly self-sufficient and interactive. However, before we move any further, let’s look at this video and get an idea on the main features of SIMs.

Watch: Main features of self-instructional materials

Source: YouTube, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RDDvzlp_Eks

Self-Help Activity 4.1: (Based on the above video)
  1. If you have designed and developed SIMs for your distance learners before, did you include these features in them?
  2. Have you noticed these features in SIMs written by other OUSL academics?

So, for an OUSL SIM to effectively support the ODL process, it must embody the following characteristics (Bates, 2015).

  • Self-Pacing: The material must allow the learner to progress at their own speed, providing both remediation (extra help) and enrichment (additional challenges) within the text.
  • Self-Contained: It must contain all the necessary information, examples, and activities required to achieve the learning outcomes of that unit. External references should be supplementary, not essential.
  • Active Learning Focus: SIMs should use techniques like embedded questions, tasks, and reflections to constantly require the learner to do something with the information, not just passively read it.
  • Clarity and Language: The language must be clear, concise, and accessible. Complex concepts must be broken down and explained using appropriate analogies and examples relevant to the Sri Lankan context where possible.
  • Structure and Signposting: Effective use of headings, bolding, bullet points, numbering, and margin notes ensures the learner can easily navigate the material and identify key takeaways.

As evidenced, the design and development of these comprehensive and self-sufficient SIMs is therefore not just a task, but the foremost service expected from an academic employed in the ODL system (as mentioned previously). It is the primary means by which you, as the subject matter expert, reach and teach your distant students.

Chapter Four · Page 3 of 7

Writing to the Distance Learner

Now that you have a general idea of what SIMs must inherently have as their essential features, we shall now elaborate on designing and developing SIMs to best suit our distance learners so that they reap the maximum benefits in their learning process. In this process, language plays a significant role in bridging the gap between you and the learner, and the following sections of this chapter will inform you how language can be manipulated to best suit the ODL system with appropriate examples.

Why must we bridge the gap? Because ………..

  • attending interactive learning sessions (ILS) is not a must.
  • your physical presence, gestures, and tone of voice must be replaced.

The voice of SIMs

It is extremely important that you use plain language because of the linguistic situation of your target group, since the language you use should be able to retain your learner’s attention. Basically, the material you write must be highly readable.

So, how can you make the SIMs you write user-friendly?

Adopt a conversational tone.

Figure 4.2

Connecting the writer’s tone with reader’s mood through conversational style

AI-generated image using Gemini.

Use personal pronouns

Say "you" for the learner and "we/I" for the teacher.

Avoid: “The reader is requested to recall how the topic of Photosynthesis was discussed in the previous session by the author.”

Instead: “You’ll remember how I mentioned photosynthesis in the previous session.”

Address the learner directly

When you are addressing your learner, move away from third person and passive voice.

Avoid: “Students are required to observe the following diagram. It is expected that the reader will identify three main components of the cell. One must ensure that the differences between plant and animal cells are noted before the next chapter is commenced.”

The above sort of writing creates a barrier and lacks personal connection.

Instead: “Now, I would like you to take a close look at this diagram. What do you notice first? As you study the image, try to pick out the three main components of the cell. Once you feel confident in identifying them, move on to the next section where we will explore the differences between plant and animal cells.”

Table 4.2
Key rules for direct addressing in SIMs
FeatureAvoid (traditionalUse (self-instructional)
PerspectiveThird person (“the learner”)Second person (“you”)
VoicePassive (“it is suggested ….”)Active (“I suggest you ……”)
ToneFormal/distantConversational/warm
Guidance Statement of factAsking questions and giving directions

Use contractions where necessary

Using contractions is one of the most effective ways to make the material feel like a spoken conversation between the teacher and learner.

Table 4.3
Contractions that could be used in SIMs
Traditional textbook styleODL “guided conversational” style
“Do not worry if ….”“Don’t worry if ….”
“It is likely that ….”“It’s likely that ….”
“We are now ready to ….”“We’re now ready to …..”
“You will see that ….”“You’ll see that ….”

However, words like “shouldn't’ve” (should not have) are too informal and can be hard for non-native speakers to decode. So, stick to simple ones like don’t, it’s, we’re, and you’ll.

Also, if a point is absolutely critical or a safety warning, sometimes the full form is better for emphasis (e.g., "Do not open the battery case" is stronger than "Don't open...").

3 / 7
Chapter Four · Page 4 of 7

Choice of words

Try avoiding surplus words because there must be clarity over clutter.

  • at the present moment in time ………………………. now
  • with a view to/in order to …………………………… to
  • owing to the fact that ……………………………….. because
  • on the grounds that …………………………………. because

Specialist vocabulary

There are certain ‘do’s and ‘don’t’s to remember when using specialist vocabulary.

  • Don’t use technical terms unnecessarily, unless they are essential.
  • Explain carefully when you introduce them.
  • Remind the reader of their meaning at appropriate times.
  • You could even use a glossary.

Sentence structure

  • Make them short and simple.
  • Use short sentences: aim for 15-20 words
  • Have one idea per paragraph.
  • Use familiar words: Choose “use" instead of “utilise," or “show" instead of “demonstrate."

Avoid: “The fact that the molecules in a liquid are closer together and thus the attractive forces between them are very much greater than the very minute forces between the molecules of a gas, is responsible for the greater resistance by a liquid to compression.”

Instead: “The molecules in a liquid are closer together than they are in a gas. As a result, the attractive forces between the liquid molecules are much greater than the very minute forces between the gas molecules. Therefore, liquids are more resistant to compression than gases.”

Use active voice and not passive

Table 4.4
Active voice counterparts of passive voice that should be used in SIMs
Passive (Avoid)Active (Use)
"The experiment should be conducted by the student now."“Now, conduct the experiment.”
“Metal beams are corroded by salt water.”“Salt water corrodes metal beams.”
“In this section, the questions will be viewed analytically.“Now, we’ll analyse the questions.”
“The reader is asked to draw a map of his/her town/village.”“You could draw a map of your own town or village.”
“The student may notice known objects in the following list.”“You’ll notice familiar objects in the list below.”

Provide a linguistic map

When the teacher is physically absent, the SIM must be a navigator to the learner; and, without such navigation, he/she may feel lost. To bring in this effect,, you could include signposts, transitional devices, and structural cues.

  • Signposting uses language to tell the student exactly where they are in their learning journey.

So, instead of saying “The next section covers the Treaty of Versailles”, you could say, “Having discussed the causes of WWI in Section 2.1, we will now examine the Treaty of Versailles to see how the peace process actually sowed the seeds for future conflict.”

  • Linguistic maps can also prepare the learner for what is coming, reducing the mental effort required to process new data.

“In this module, we will first define X, then contrast it with Y, and finally apply both to a real-world case study.”

  • They can stimulate a dialogue as well.

Inserting rhetorical questions or directional phrases like, “You might be wondering why we ignored factor Z…” or “Pause here for a moment and look back at Table 4.3.”

  • Linguistic cues can be used to indicate the changes in tone or gestures of a teacher when emphasising a point.

Using explicit markers like, “Crucially…”, “The most vital takeaway here is…”, or “Note that this formula differs from the one in Session 1.”

The following table will give you a clearer idea about what happens when you use linguistic maps in the SIMs you write.

Table 4.5
Impact of linguistic mapping on the distance learner’s experience
FeatureWithout mappingWith linguistic mapping
FlowAbrupt transitions between topicsSmooth and logical connection between sections
OrientationLearner forgets the main objectiveConstant reminders of the main topic
PacingMonotonous density of textStrategic pauses, summaries, and emphasis
OutcomeHigh frustration and dropout riskIncreased confidence and self-regulation

Chapter Four · Page 5 of 7

Spelling

The standard practice at the OUSL is adhering to British English. This consistency ensures professionalism and aligns with the academic traditions of the Commonwealth.

Here are the most common categories where British English differs from American English, with examples relevant to instructional design:

  • The “-ise” vs. “-ize” suffix

British: Organise, summarise, recognise, characterise

American: Organize, summarize, recognize, characterize

  • The “-our” vs. “-or” ending

British: Behaviour, colour, neighbour, flavour

American: Behavior, color, neighbor, flavor

  • Doubling consonants

British: Modelled, travelling, cancelled, counselling

American: Modeled, traveling, canceled, counseling

  • “-re” vs. “-er” endings

British: Centre, theatre, libre, litre

American: Center, theater, liber, liter

  • Have a look at the following table as well for extra knowledge.
Table 4.6
British vs. American English: for further knowledge
British (use this)
✅		American (avoid this)❎
HaemoglobinHemoglobin
FoetusFetus
EnrolmentEnrollment
AnalogueAnalog
FulfilFulfill
ProgrammeProgram
AgeingAging
LicenceLicense

Capitalisation

In ODL materials, over-capitalisation is a common issue that can actually make it harder for the learner to identify proper nouns or the start of new sentences.

  • Common nouns vs. proper nouns

Incorrect: The Students must submit their Assignments to the Regional Centre.

Correct: The students must submit their assignments to the Regional Centre.

Why: “Students” and “assignments” are general categories (common nouns), while “Regional Centre” is a specific OUSL entity (proper noun).

  • Academic subjects and disciplines

Incorrect: I am interested in studying Psychology and Social Sciences.

Correct: I am interested in studying psychology and social sciences.

Exception: “I am enrolled in PLU3301: Introduction to Psychology.” (Here, it is a specific course title).

  • Titles and roles

Incorrect: You should consult your Tutor or the Senior Lecturer for guidance.

Correct: You should consult your tutor or the senior lecturer for guidance.

Correct (Specific): “Please forward your request to Senior Lecturer Dr. Perera.”

  • Components of the SIM

Incorrect: Please refer to the Learning Outcomes and Activities in the next Chapter.

Correct: Please refer to the learning outcomes and activities in the next session.

Exception: “As stated in Session 4, the results were…” (Used as a specific label).

5 / 7
Chapter Four · Page 6 of 7

Punctuation

In ODL materials, punctuation acts as a “silent tutor”. Since the learners cannot hear your pauses or see your emphasis, punctuation marks must guide them through the text to prevent fatigue and misunderstanding. Precise punctuation is critical because many learners may be reading in their second or third language, and clear punctuation clarifies complex academic arguments.

  • Serial comma (Oxford comma)

Ambiguous: “The module covers developmental psychology, child health and safety and nutrition.” (Is 'safety and nutrition' one combined topic or two separate ones?)

Clear (British): “The module covers developmental psychology, child health, and safety and nutrition.”

Importance: It ensures the learner knows exactly how many distinct topics they need to master.

  • Using colons and semicolons for logical flow

Semicolons are excellent for linking two closely related ideas without the use of a full stop, but keeping the instructional flow moving.

Correct use: “Do not move on to Activity 4 yet; you must first complete the self-assessment on page 20.”

The Colon: Use it to introduce a list or a defining statement.

  • “The experiment requires three components: a beaker, distilled water, and a thermometer.”
  • Hyphens vs. Dashes

Incorrect use of dashes can make a text look cluttered or unprofessional.

Hyphens (-): Use for compound words or modifiers.

  • Example: “A well-structured session,” or “A second-year student.”

En-dashes (–): Use for ranges (dates, pages, or values).

  • Example: “Read pages 45–67,” or “The 2024–2025 academic year.”

Em-dashes (—): Used sparingly in SIMs to add an abrupt emphasis or an aside—like this—though ODL writers often prefer brackets or commas for a smoother feel.

  • Question mark

Since SIMs are essentially written in a conversational tone, question marks are vital for engaging the learner’s meta-cognition.

Example: “Have you ever wondered why some metals rust faster than others? In this section, we will find out.”

Note: Always ensure the question mark is placed inside the quotation marks if the question is part of the quote, but outside if it is part of the main sentence.

Chapter Five · Page 2 of 12

The Role of Multimedia in ODL

In ODL, multimedia helps bridge the gap between the teacher and the learner by making learning more engaging, flexible, and accessible. Since learners often study independently and at different times and locations, audio, video, animations, simulations, and interactive activities can help explain complex ideas more clearly than text alone. Well-designed multimedia resources can create a sense of connection, support different learning preferences, and encourage active participation.

Think about it

Have you ever watched an educational video that kept your attention from beginning to end? What made it effective? Was it the presenter, the visuals, the pace, the examples, or the way the content was organised?

Now think about a video that failed to engage you. Why did you stop watching?

Chapter Five · Page 3 of 12

Selecting Appropriate Media Formats

Figure 5.1

Guide to selecting appropriate media formats

Audio
Concept introduction and review
  • Short introductions
  • Reviewing learned content
Video
Demonstrations and processes
  • Show steps visually
  • How-to procedures
Animation
Complex theories and workflows
  • Show what cannot be seen
  • Show cause and effect
Interactive multimedia
Practice and decision-making
  • Quizzes and knowledge checks
  • Branching scenarios
The key: select media that supports the learning outcome, not technology for its own sake.

Choosing the right media format depends on what you want learners to achieve. Not every topic needs a video or animation. A short audio explanation may work well for introducing a concept, while a demonstration or process-based topic may require video. Interactive multimedia such as quizzes, simulations, and branching activities can be useful when learners need to practise skills or make decisions. The key is to select media that supports the learning outcome rather than using technology simply because it is available.

Strengths and Limitations of Multimedia Learning

Multimedia learning can make learning more meaningful by combining words, images, sound, and interaction. It can simplify complex concepts, provide real-world examples, increase learner motivation, and allow learners to review materials at their own pace. However, poorly designed multimedia can create confusion and increase cognitive load. Too much text, unnecessary animations, distracting sounds, or complex interfaces may reduce learning effectiveness. Therefore, effective multimedia resources should be carefully planned, learner-centred, accessible, and designed according to sound instructional principles.

Chapter Five · Page 4 of 12

Principles

This section presents the instructional design principles that underpin effective multimedia learning.

Do you agree that;

Multimedia should help learners understand—not simply provide more information.

Key principles include:

Figure 5.2

Key principles of developing audio, video, and interactive multimedia resources

1
Learner-centred design
  • Understand your audience
  • Design for their needs
2
Alignment with learning outcomes
  • Clear purpose
  • Content supports the outcome
3
Conversational communication
  • Friendly, informal tone
  • Speak to the learner
4
Cognitive load management
  • Avoid overload
  • Remove clutter
5
Multimedia learning principles
  • Combine words and pictures
  • Leave out extra material
6
Storytelling for learning
  • Build a narrative
  • Link to real situations
7
Learner engagement and interaction
  • Active participation
  • Practise skills
8
Accessibility and universal design
  • Design for all learners
  • Provide alternatives
9
Consistency across media
  • A unified experience
  • Common layout and terms

The following principles provide a practical foundation for designing effective audio, video, and interactive multimedia resources for ODL. Each principle is presented with a brief explanation, a real educational example, common mistakes to avoid, recommended practices, and a reflective question to help you apply the concept in your own teaching.

Explanation

Effective multimedia begins with the learner, not the technology. Design decisions should reflect learners' prior knowledge, learning needs, digital literacy, and the context in which they study. ODL learners often study independently and at different times, so multimedia should support self-paced learning and encourage active engagement.

Example

A biology lecturer develops a series of short five-minute videos, each explaining a single concept using simple language, labelled diagrams, and self-check questions. Students can watch the videos individually whenever they need revision.

Common Mistakes
  • Designing multimedia based on what the teacher wants to present rather than what learners need.
  • Including too much information in a single resource.
  • Assuming all learners have the same background knowledge or internet access.
Recommended Practice
  • Identify learner needs before selecting media.
  • Focus on one learning objective at a time.
  • Provide opportunities for learners to pause, reflect, and revisit concepts.
  • Design for independent study and flexible learning.
Think about it…

Think about one of your current multimedia resources. Does it focus on what learners need to learn, or on everything you want to teach?

Explanation

Every multimedia resource should have a clear purpose. Audio, video, or interactive activities should directly support the intended learning outcomes rather than serving as additional or optional content.

Example

Instead of recording a one-hour lecture, an economics lecturer creates a short animated video demonstrating how supply and demand curves change under different market conditions, directly supporting the learning outcome of interpreting economic graphs.

Common Mistakes
  • Creating videos simply because multimedia is available.
  • Including interesting but unrelated information.
  • Using multimedia that does not contribute to assessment or learning activities.
Recommended Practice
  • Begin with clearly defined learning outcomes.
  • Select the media format that best supports those outcomes.
  • Ensure activities and assessments reinforce the multimedia resource.
Think about it…

Can you explain how each multimedia resource in your course helps learners achieve a specific learning outcome?

Explanation

Learners respond more positively to multimedia that speaks directly to them in a friendly and supportive tone. Conversational language creates a sense of instructor presence and reduces the feeling of studying alone.

Example

A video lesson begins with, "Have you ever wondered why eclipses occur? Let's explore this fascinating phenomenon together." The presenter explains concepts naturally, as if speaking directly to one learner.

Common Mistakes
  • Reading academic text word-for-word.
  • Using overly formal or technical language.
  • Speaking too quickly or without variation in tone.
Recommended Practice
  • Write scripts as if speaking to one learner.
  • Use clear, simple language.
  • Ask questions that encourage learners to think before providing explanations.
  • Maintain an enthusiastic and supportive tone.
Think about it…

If you listened to your own narration, would it sound like a conversation or a formal lecture?

Explanation

Learners have limited working memory. Multimedia should reduce unnecessary mental effort so learners can focus on understanding the essential concepts.

Example

A chemistry animation introduces one reaction step at a time, with narration explaining only the current visual instead of displaying multiple diagrams simultaneously.

Common Mistakes
  • Overcrowded slides.
  • Long videos covering many topics.
  • Simultaneous narration, animations, background music, and extensive on-screen text.
  • Decorative graphics that distract from learning.
Recommended Practice
  • Present one idea at a time.
  • Keep videos short and focused.
  • Use signalling to highlight important information.
  • Eliminate unnecessary visuals and sounds.
  • Allow learners to pause and review sections.
Think about it…

Could your multimedia resource be simplified without reducing learners' understanding?

Explanation

Effective multimedia combines words, visuals, and audio in ways that support learning. Learners understand concepts better when information is presented using complementary visual and verbal channels rather than relying on text alone.

Example

A geography lesson explains volcanic eruptions using animation with narrated explanations instead of lengthy paragraphs of text.

Common Mistakes
  • Reading exactly what appears on screen.
  • Displaying large blocks of text during narration.
  • Using unrelated images that do not support learning.
Recommended Practice
  • Combine narration with meaningful visuals.
  • Replace unnecessary text with diagrams or animations.
  • Use images that directly support the explanation.
  • Keep layouts simple and uncluttered.
Think about it…

Do your visuals help explain the concept, or are they simply decorative?

Explanation

Stories make learning meaningful by connecting concepts to real-life situations. A well-designed narrative captures attention, improves understanding, and enhances long-term retention.

Example

A public health lesson begins with the story of a family responding to a disease outbreak before introducing disease prevention strategies.

Common Mistakes
  • Presenting facts without context.
  • Including stories that are entertaining but unrelated to learning outcomes.
  • Allowing the story to overshadow the learning objectives.
Recommended Practice
  • Use authentic scenarios and case studies.
  • Connect stories directly to learning outcomes.
  • Encourage learners to analyse situations and propose solutions.
Think about it…

Could a real-life story help learners better understand this topic?

Explanation

Learning improves when learners actively participate rather than passively watch or listen. Multimedia should encourage thinking, questioning, analysing, and applying knowledge.

Example

During an instructional video, learners are asked to pause, predict the outcome of an experiment, and compare their predictions with the demonstration.

Common Mistakes
  • Long videos with no learner interaction.
  • Presenting information without opportunities for reflection.
  • Treating multimedia as passive content delivery.
Recommended Practice
  • Include pause-and-think questions.
  • Add short quizzes or interactive checkpoints.
  • Encourage note-taking and reflection.
  • Integrate multimedia with discussions and practical activities.
Think about it…

How often does your multimedia resource invite learners to think or respond rather than simply watch?

Explanation

Multimedia should be accessible to all learners, including those with disabilities, different learning preferences, or limited access to technology. Inclusive design ensures that every learner has an equitable opportunity to participate.

Example

An educational video includes captions, a downloadable transcript, high-contrast visuals, and clear narration, allowing learners to choose the format that best suits their needs.

Common Mistakes
  • Publishing videos without captions.
  • Using colours that are difficult to distinguish.
  • Ignoring mobile users or learners with low-bandwidth internet.
Recommended Practice
  • Provide captions and transcripts.
  • Use clear fonts and sufficient colour contrast.
  • Ensure multimedia functions well on different devices.
  • Offer alternative formats where possible.
Think about it…

Would every learner in your course be able to access and benefit from this multimedia resource?

Explanation

Learners should experience a coherent learning journey regardless of whether they are reading print materials, watching videos, listening to audio, or participating in LMS activities. Consistent design reduces confusion and helps learners focus on learning.

Example

A course uses the same learning outcomes, terminology, visual style, icons, and sequence of topics in the study guide, videos, podcasts, and LMS activities.

Common Mistakes
  • Using different terminology across learning materials.
  • Changing layouts, colours, or navigation styles between resources.
  • Presenting contradictory information in different media.
Recommended Practice
  • Develop a consistent visual identity for the course.
  • Use common terminology and instructional language.
  • Align multimedia resources with print materials and LMS activities.
  • Maintain a consistent structure throughout all learning resources.
Think about it…

If learners moved between your printed study guide, video lessons, and LMS, would they experience one coherent course or several disconnected resources?

Bringing the Principles Together

These principles are most effective when applied collectively rather than in isolation. Before developing any multimedia resource, ask yourself:

  • Is it learner-centred?
  • Does it support the intended learning outcomes?
  • Is the communication clear and conversational?
  • Have I minimised unnecessary cognitive load?
  • Do the visuals and audio work together to enhance understanding?
  • Does the resource engage learners actively?
  • Is it accessible to all learners?
  • Is it consistent with the rest of the course?

Keeping these questions in mind throughout the design process will help you create multimedia resources that are engaging, inclusive, and educationally effective.

Process

This section presents a practical workflow for designing multimedia resources suitable for ODL.

Rather than viewing media production as a technical activity, the guide emphasises an instructional design process.

The process includes:

  • analysing learner needs;
  • identifying learning outcomes;
  • selecting appropriate media;
  • preparing scripts;
  • developing storyboards;
  • planning production;
  • recording audio and video;
  • editing multimedia;
  • integrating interactive elements;
  • reviewing educational effectiveness;
  • conducting quality assurance; and
  • evaluating learner feedback.

Each stage concludes with a Checkpoint.

Example:

Checkpoint

Before recording your video, ask yourself:

  • Are the learning outcomes clear?
  • Is every scene necessary?
  • Does every visual support learning?
  • Have you avoided unnecessary information?
  • Can learners easily follow the sequence?

Chapter Five · Page 7 of 12

Understanding the Multimedia Production Process

Creating an educational video may seem like a complex task, but it becomes much more manageable when you follow a structured production process. Like building a house, successful multimedia production begins with careful planning before any recording takes place.

The production process consists of three main stages: pre-production, production, and post-production. Each stage has a specific purpose, and together they help ensure that your final multimedia resource is engaging, accurate, and aligned with your learning outcomes.

Pre-production is where most of the important decisions are made. This is the planning stage, during which you identify your learning outcomes, decide on the most appropriate way to present the content, prepare your script, develop a storyboard, and organise the resources, equipment, and locations needed for recording. Investing time in planning will save considerable time and effort later in the production process.

Once you have completed your planning, you move to the production stage. This is where your ideas come to life. You record your narration, capture video footage, create demonstrations, interview subject experts if required, and collect any images or other media that will be included in your learning resource. Remember that good production is about more than using a high-quality camera—it is about communicating clearly and keeping learners engaged.

After recording is complete, the project enters post-production. During this stage, the individual audio and video components are assembled into a coherent learning resource. You will edit the recordings, remove unnecessary sections, improve sound quality, add titles, captions, graphics, animations, transitions, background music (where appropriate), and any other visual elements that enhance understanding. This is also the stage where you review the overall flow of the resource and ensure that it effectively supports the intended learning outcomes.

Throughout all three stages, it is important to monitor the quality of your work. Rather than waiting until the end of the project, review your multimedia resource regularly using the Quality Assurance (QA) Checklist provided in this guide. The checklist will help you verify that your resource meets institutional standards for instructional quality, technical production, accessibility, and learner engagement before it is shared with students.

To support your work, examples of a video script template, storyboard, and Quality Assurance Checklist are provided in the following pages. These tools are designed to help you plan, organise, and evaluate your multimedia resources systematically, ensuring that every production is purposeful, learner-centred, and ready for use in an ODL environment.

Reflect

Before you begin recording, ask yourself:

Have I clearly planned what learners need to see, hear, and do to achieve the intended learning outcomes?

Chapter Five · Page 8 of 12

Writing a Two-Column Educational Video Script

A two-column script is the industry-standard tool used by instructional designers and media creators to bridge the gap between an educational concept and a finished video asset. By splitting the page cleanly down the middle, it separates what the learner sees from what the learner hears, ensuring both channels work in perfect harmony.

The Anatomy of the Columns

The Left Column (VIDEO): This side houses all visual instructions. It includes camera angles (e.g., wide shot, close-up), on-screen actions, slide or interface captures, animations, and exact placeholders for On-Screen Text (OST) or lower-third graphics.

The Right Column (AUDIO): This side contains everything the audience will hear. It features the spoken narration (written in a natural, conversational tone), character dialogue, and explicit technical cues for Sound Effects (SFX) and Background Music (BGM).

Why It’s Vital for Instructional Design

Enforces the Modality Principle: According to cognitive load theory, learners process visual and auditory information through separate channels. A two-column layout allows you to check at a glance that your narration directly complements the on-screen graphics rather than competing with them, preventing cognitive overload.

Streamlines Production Tracking: It acts as a unified contract for the production team. The voiceover talent can read the right column seamlessly without getting distracted by technical jargon, while the video editor can use the left column as a checklist to anchor visuals to specific spoken words.

Controls Pacing and Timing: Because humans speak at an average rate of 130 to 150 words per minute, placing narration next to visual descriptions makes it incredibly easy to judge the real-time pacing of a scene. If a complex visual layout only has five words of audio next to it, the script instantly signals that the scene is moving too fast for the learner to absorb the information.

Video Script Template

Project Title: [Insert Title, e.g., Introduction to Multimodal Learning]

Module/Topic: [Insert Module, e.g., Learn → Observe → Try → Reflect]

Target Run Time: [e.g., 2:00 Minutes]

Version/Date: [e.g., V1.0 - July 2026]

VIDEO (Visuals, Graphics, Screen Actions)AUDIO (Narration, Dialogue, Sound & Music)

[SCENE 1: Opening Slides]

Slide 1: Video Title

Slide 2: Learning outcomes

[AUDIO ELEMENTS]

Background Music

[SCENE 2: INTRO / HOOK]

• Visual: Wide shot of a modern, clean workspace. A laptop displays a pulsing lightbulb icon.

• On-Screen Text (Lower Third): Welcome to Multimodal Design.

• Animation: Text fades in smoothly from the left.

[AUDIO ELEMENTS]

• [BGM]: Upbeat, inspiring electronic music starts low, then ducks under the narration.

• NARRATOR (V.O.): "Ever wonder why some online courses stick while others are instantly forgotten? It all comes down to how we design the experience."

[SCENE 3: THE PROBLEM]

• Visual: Medium shot of a student looking overwhelmed, staring at a screen filled with dense blocks of text.

• Animation: Camera slowly zooms in on the student to emphasize the feeling of cognitive overload.

• [SFX]: A slight, low-pitched hum to simulate digital fatigue.

• NARRATOR (V.O.): "Dumping text on a page forces the brain to work twice as hard. But text isn't your only tool."

[SCENE 4: INTRODUCTION OF CONCEPT]

• Visual: Screen transitions to a clean, minimalist 4-quadrant graphic showing four icons:

1. Book (Learn)

2. Eye/Magnifying Glass (Observe)

3. Pencil/Gears (Try)

4. Mirror/Checkmark (Reflect)

• Action: The "Learn" quadrant lights up first.

• [BGM]: Music shifts to a brighter, more focused tempo.

• NARRATOR (V.O.): "By structuring your delivery through a consistent learning pattern—Learn, Observe, Try, and Reflect—you move your learners from passive reading to active mastery."

[SCENE 5: DEMONSTRATION / SCREENSHARE]

• Visual: Direct screen capture of a Learning Management System (LMS) dashboard.

• Action: A digital mouse cursor clicks on a video link titled "Watch This Case Study." A call-out circle highlights the click area.

• [SFX]: Crisp digital mouse click sound.

• NARRATOR (V.O.): "For example, in the 'Observe' phase, don't just tell them the rules. Show them a real-world video example and ask them to analyze how the visuals complement the voiceover."

[SCENE 6: CALL TO ACTION / OUTRO]

• Visual: Return to the main screen graphic. The final quadrant ("Reflect") glows.

• On-Screen Text: URL or Next Steps (e.g., Proceed to Module 2: Try It).

• Visual: Logo of the ODL Institute fades in at the center.

• NARRATOR (V.O.): "Now it's your turn. Head over to the workspace, review the worked examples, and prepare to script your very first two-minute video. Happy designing!"

• [BGM]: Music swells up for 3 seconds, then fades out completely.

Key Tips for Writing Your Script

  • Keep Audio Conversational: Write the right column exactly how a human naturally speaks, not like an academic textbook. Use contractions (e.g., don't, it's, you're).
  • Time Your Words: As a rule of thumb, humans speak roughly 130 to 150 words per minute. A two-minute video should have no more than 260–300 words of narration.
  • Explicit Cues: Always use brackets like [SFX] (Sound Effects) or [BGM] (Background Music) to give your audio editor clear instructions on when to add or change sound elements.

Chapter Five · Page 9 of 12

Creating Storyboard

A storyboard serves as the visual blueprint for an educational video, mapping out the entire lesson shot-by-shot before production begins. Much like a comic strip, it bridges the gap between your written script and the final media asset, ensuring that every visual choice serves a pedagogical purpose.

Why It Matters in Instructional Design

Guarantees Alignment: It forces you to verify that your on-screen graphics, animations, and text directly support the intended learning outcomes rather than just acting as superficial decorations.

Manages Cognitive Load: By planning exactly when and where visuals appear alongside the voiceover, you can prevent split-attention effects and avoid overwhelming the learner's working memory.

Saves Time and Budget: It provides video editors, animators, and voice talent with an unambiguous roadmap, drastically reducing costly revisions and trial-and-error during post-production.

The Core Pillars of an Educational Frame

When building a storyboard for online learning, each frame typically splits into four essential components:

1. The Visual Frame: A rough sketch, wireframe, or reference photo showing what the viewer will see on screen (e.g., a teacher, an interface demonstration, or a conceptual model).

2. Narration & Audio Cues: The spoken script paired with crucial auditory instructions, such as sound effects (SFX) or background music adjustments (BGM).

3. On-Screen Text & Graphics: Placeholders for charts, text callouts, or mathematical equations that reinforce the spoken word.

4. Technical Notes: Clear directives for the production team regarding camera angles, pacing, animations, or user interface (UI) transitions.

Chapter Five · Page 10 of 12

Quality Assurance Checklist

The quality assurance process for educational video productions focuses on three key areas:

✓ Content/Narrative Structure: Evaluating the clarity, flow, and organization of the content.

✓ Pedagogical Approach: Evaluating student engagement, cognitive load, and active learning strategies.

✓ Production Quality: Evaluating technical excellence in video, audio, and materials.

This structured approach ensures high-quality videos as impactful learning resources. Please refer the QA checklist at every stage of the production.

Criteria

(A) Clarity of Content

  1. The objectives/learning outcomes are mentioned at the beginning of the video.
  2. The content aligns with the relevant objectives/learning outcomes.
  3. The content is clear, accurate, and well-organized

(B) Flow of the Video Narrative

  1. The video follows a logical and coherent sequence of ideas/concepts.
  2. Transitions between segments are smooth and easy to follow.
  3. The content is free of redundant or irrelevant information.

(C) Structure of the Video (Beginning-Middle-End)

  1. The video begins with a clear introduction and an engaging hook.
  2. The core content is presented effectively with examples and explanations.
  3. The video ends with a clear summary or call for action.
Criteria

(A) Cognitive Load

  1. Complex topics are broken into manageable sections.
  2. The video avoids excessive text or visuals that could overwhelm learners.
  3. Language is simple, and explanations are concise.

(B) Student Engagement

  1. Visuals, animations, or examples are engaging and relevant.
  2. The video includes prompts or questions to encourage critical thinking.
  3. The tone is conversational and engaging for learners.

(C) Active Learning

  1. The video includes pauses, questions, or activities to promote interaction.
  2. Real-world applications or scenarios are included to demonstrate concepts.
  3. The video encourages learners to take notes/engage in follow-up activities
Criteria

(A) Video Quality

  1. The video resolution is clear and suitable.
  2. Lighting and visuals are consistent, with no shadows or overexposure.
  3. Transitions are smooth and free from abrupt cuts.
  4. The video is free of distractions (e.g., shaky footage, background clutter).

(B) Audio Quality

  1. The audio is clear, with no distortions or background noise.
  2. Audio and video are synchronized accurately.
  3. Volume levels are consistent throughout the video.

(C) Quality of Other Materials

  1. Graphics, animations, and visual aids are clear and in good quality.
  2. Images and visuals are free of pixelation or low resolution.
  3. Captions and subtitles are accurate and well- aligned with spoken content.

(D) Copyrights and Avoiding Plagiarism

  1. Resources used (images, music, videos...etc.) comply with copyright laws.
  2. Openly licensed materials (OER) or royalty-free resources are used appropriately.
  3. Proper credits and citations are provided for external materials.
  4. The video is original and free of plagiarism.

Practice

This section focuses on applying the concepts presented in this chapter through authentic multimedia design tasks. Rather than testing theoretical knowledge, the activities encourage you to analyse, design, create, evaluate, and reflect on multimedia learning resources that can be integrated into your own courses. As you complete each activity, apply the principles of learner-centred design, alignment with learning outcomes, effective communication, accessibility, and multimedia learning.

Suggested activities include:

Analyse: Evaluate an existing educational video using the multimedia design checklist.

Design: Develop learning outcomes and prepare a storyboard for a short multimedia lesson.

Create: Produce a 3–5 minute educational video or audio resource for one topic in your own course.

Review: Exchange multimedia resources with a colleague and provide constructive feedback using the quality rubric.

Reflect: Consider the following questions:

  • What instructional decisions were most challenging?
  • Which multimedia principles were easiest to apply?
  • How effectively does your resource support independent learning?
  • How could learner interaction be improved?
  • What revisions would you make before using the resource with students?

LMS Course Design and Development introduces the principles and practice of building effective online courses in a Learning Management System (LMS). You will learn how to:

This chapter gives you the principles and resources to build materials made for LMS delivery.

6.7 Assessment and Feedback

Assessment shows whether learners have met the outcomes. Feedback helps them improve.

What is an LMS-based assessment?

An LMS-based assessment is an assessment task that learners complete, and that you mark and give feedback on, through the LMS. The share of continuous assessment (CA) marks that comes from LMS-based assessments depends on the course type. It is 61%–100% in a fully LMS-based course and 20%–60% in a blended course. It does not apply to supplemental courses.

Chapter Seven

Integrating Generative AI into Multimodal Instructional Material Development

Page 1 of 9

Introduction

In ODL, learners depend largely on the course material to develop knowledge and skills, since they study with limited contact with the teacher. The quality of this material therefore has a direct effect on their learning. Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers academics a means of supporting the development of such material. It can be used to draft explanations, generate examples, design learner activities, and improve the clarity of written text, which reduces the time required to prepare a first draft (Kasneci et al., 2023; Lo, 2023).

Generative AI is intended to assist the academic, not to replace the academic’s role. Decisions on learning outcomes, content, and compliance with institutional standards remain the responsibility of the academic. All AI-generated output should therefore be treated as a draft and reviewed carefully before it is included in the official course material (Giannakos et al., 2025).

  • Explain the role of generative AI in developing ODL course materials, together with its benefits and its limitations.
  • Apply prompt engineering techniques, including role, contextual, few-shot, iterative, and chained prompting, to generate course content.
  • Use generative AI to plan lessons and to draft explanations, worked examples, case studies, and learner activities.
  • Generate formative assessment items and supporting visual or multimedia resources with the assistance of generative AI.
  • Select an appropriate generative AI tool for a given stage of course development.
  • Critically review AI-generated content for academic accuracy, pedagogical appropriateness, and alignment with learning outcomes.

Chapter Seven · Page 2 of 9

Key Concepts

This section defines the key terms used in this chapter in relation to generative AI.

Generative Artificial Intelligence

An AI system that produces new text, images, presentations, or other content in response to user instructions, based on patterns learned from large collections of data.

Prompt

The instruction given to a generative AI system describing the task, the intended audience, the educational context, and the expected format of the response.

Prompt Engineering

The practice of designing prompts deliberately and iteratively to improve the relevance, accuracy, and educational value of the output.

Iterative Prompting

The development of a lesson through a sequence of smaller prompts, in which each prompt refines or extends the previous output, instead of requesting the complete lesson at once.

Prompt Chaining

An extension of iterative prompting in which the output of one prompt is used as the input for the next, so that the outline, explanations, examples, and activities form a connected sequence.

Academic Validation

The process by which an academic reviews AI-generated content for technical accuracy, pedagogical appropriateness, and curriculum alignment before use.

AI Hallucination

An instance in which a generative AI system produces information, a reference, or a claim that appears plausible and is stated with confidence, but is inaccurate or fabricated (Ji et al., 2023).

Figure 7.1
How the Four Core Concepts Build on Each Other
Note. The four terms describe increasing levels of structure, from a single instruction through to a fully connected sequence of linked prompts.
2 / 9
Chapter Seven · Page 3 of 9

The AI-Assisted Course Development Cycle

Generative AI can support every stage of lesson development, in addition to the writing itself. Figure 7.2 shows how these stages are connected and where the academic’s review takes place in the cycle. This review applies to each of the sections that follow.

Figure 7.2
Six Stages of AI-Assisted Course Development
Note. The six stages cycle clockwise around a constant of academic review and judgement.

Effective ODL material does more than present information. A learner who studies independently needs opportunities to apply concepts, reflect on their own understanding, and relate theory to practice. For this reason, worked examples, activities, case studies, and assessments should be included in almost every lesson. Generative AI can produce a draft set of these elements from a single prompt, which enables the academic to develop a complete and consistent learning unit in less time.

Select a stage below to view the guidance and a sample prompt.

Careful planning at the outset is important, since a well-sequenced lesson provides the learner with a clear path through the content. Generative AI can suggest alternative sequences, such as a problem-based structure in place of a purely linear one, and identify the prerequisite knowledge a learner requires before proceeding to more advanced content. These suggestions should be reviewed before they are adopted.

Figure 7.3
Linear Versus Problem-Based Sequencing of the Same Four Topics
Note. The same four topics can be arranged as a straightforward linear sequence or reordered around a real-world scenario, depending on which better suits the learning outcome.

Generative AI can also assist in refining learning outcomes by suggesting measurable action verbs and identifying outcomes that exceed what the lesson can realistically achieve. Such suggestions should be checked against the curriculum and the learner group before they are adopted.

Lesson outline prompt
You are an instructional designer at the OUSL. Develop a lesson for first-year undergraduate students studying through ODL. The lesson should include an introduction, clearly stated learning outcomes, learner-friendly explanations, worked examples, reflection questions, self-assessment activities, and a concise summary. Use clear academic language suitable for independent learners.
Planning activity

Select one lesson that you are developing or revising. Generate a lesson outline that includes an introduction, learning outcomes, main topics, learner activities, and self-assessment questions. Compare it with your existing plan and make the necessary revisions before proceeding.

Once the structure has been finalised, generative AI can assist in developing the content. It is particularly useful for adapting an explanation to a given audience. When the learner profile, level of study, and intended outcome are provided, the same concept can be explained differently for postgraduate learners and for first-year undergraduates, while the core concept remains unchanged.

Generative AI is also useful when it is difficult to begin writing. The academic may request several alternative introductions or summaries and adapt the most suitable one. The quality of the output depends on the detail provided in the prompt; therefore, the prompt should specify the subject, audience, style, length, and any instructional elements required.

Generative AI can also produce examples and analogies that make abstract ideas concrete. Where possible, these examples should be adapted to the Sri Lankan context. Each analogy should be checked carefully, since an analogy that is slightly inaccurate may create a misconception instead of correcting one.

Content development prompt
You are an experienced instructional designer developing course materials for undergraduate students studying through ODL. Prepare a lesson on climate change and its effects suitable for first-year learners with limited prior knowledge. The lesson should include an engaging introduction, measurable learning outcomes, learner-friendly explanations, two worked examples, one real-world case study, a reflection activity, three self-assessment questions with answers, and a concise summary.
Good practice

Request complete learning experiences rather than content alone: explanations together with examples, activities, reflection questions, and assessment tasks.

Worked examples show learners how a theoretical concept is applied in practice. In an ODL setting, where most learners study the material independently, a well-constructed example carries much of the explanation. It demonstrates the reasoning before the learner attempts a similar task without assistance, which reduces the cognitive load placed on a novice learner (Sweller, 1988). Generative AI can produce several examples in different contexts, from which the most suitable one can be selected.

For instance, a lesson on calculating compound interest could use examples from a personal savings account, a small business loan, or a housing loan. Reviewing several examples allows the academic to select the one that best supports the learning outcomes and suits the local context.

Worked example prompt
Develop a worked example showing how to calculate compound interest on a fixed deposit over three years. Explain each step clearly, show the formula and each calculation, and point out common errors learners make. The explanation should be suitable for first-year undergraduate students studying independently.

Case studies require learners to apply theory to a realistic situation. While a worked example shows how a problem is solved, a case study requires learners to analyse the situation themselves, consider alternative solutions, and justify their choice. Generative AI can draft realistic scenarios based on professional practice in a wide range of disciplines.

For example, an education course might examine technology-enhanced learning in a rural school, and a management course might examine organisational change in a public sector institution. Such scenarios develop critical thinking and decision-making skills; however, academics should review them carefully to ensure that they reflect local professional practice.

Activities encourage learners to engage with the material rather than only read it. Generative AI can produce a range of activities, such as reflection questions, concept-mapping exercises, problem-solving tasks, and discussion questions for an online forum, which help independent learners to remain actively engaged. It can also be instructed to apply the revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Krathwohl, 2002), so that activities develop higher-order thinking skills in addition to recall.

Figure 7.4
Bloom’s Taxonomy Applied to Activity Design
Note. Activities should be requested across all six levels of the taxonomy, not only the two or three that are easiest to write.

Instead of placing all activities at the end of a lesson, shorter activities may be distributed throughout the content, giving learners regular opportunities to pause and consolidate their understanding.

Learner activity prompt
Generate three learner-centred activities for a lesson on solid waste management in the community. Include one reflection activity, one problem-solving activity, and one collaborative online discussion task suitable for undergraduate students studying through ODL.

Self-assessment enables learners to monitor their own progress without waiting for feedback from a tutor. Generative AI can produce a variety of question formats, including multiple-choice, true or false, matching, short-answer, and scenario-based questions, each accompanied by an explanation of why an answer is correct or incorrect.

Figure 7.5
Five Formative Assessment Formats Generative AI Can Produce
Note. Each format is paired with a written explanation of the answer, rather than a mark alone.

Assessment questions should always be reviewed carefully. The academic should verify their technical accuracy, ensure that only one option is clearly correct where appropriate, and confirm that each question measures the intended learning outcome rather than simple memorisation.

A diagram can often present a relationship more clearly than a paragraph of text. Generative AI can suggest an appropriate diagram, prepare a description for an illustrator, or propose a suitable way of representing a concept visually. Tools such as Napkin AI can convert a written explanation into a simple concept diagram, while Canva Magic Studio and Gamma can generate slide layouts from a text prompt. These tools assist with design, but the academic decides what the visual should show. The licence terms of any AI-generated image should be checked before it is included in course material.

The same approach applies to multimedia resources. Generative AI can assist with video scripts, narration, podcast outlines, and storyboards. For example, after completing a lesson on water conservation, an academic could request a five-minute video script summarising the key concepts, and then adapt and record it as a supplementary resource.
