Chapter Seven · Page 4 of 9

7.8 Prompt Engineering

The quality of the output depends largely on the quality of the prompt. An effective prompt usually includes six elements: the role the AI should adopt, the target learners, the educational context, the intended learning outcomes, the writing style, and the expected format. Figure 7.6 presents these six elements, and Figure 7.7 shows how the five techniques described in this section build on one another.

Figure 7.6
Anatomy of an Effective Prompt
Note. A prompt that specifies all six elements needs less revision than one that leaves the AI to guess the audience, context, or expected format.
Figure 7.7
Relationship Among the Five Prompting Techniques
Note. Role, contextual, and few-shot prompting act as components. Iterative prompting repeats them across a series of smaller requests, and prompt chaining links those repeats into a single connected pipeline.
Watch: Mastering Prompt Engineering for Teachers

Source: YouTube, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tZKzDG5g79Q

A demonstration of how to construct effective prompts, covering the techniques described below.

In role prompting, the AI is assigned a specific identity, such as an instructional designer or a subject matter expert, before the task is given. This helps the output to follow an educational register rather than a general, encyclopaedic one.

Prompt
You are an experienced instructional designer at the OUSL. Develop a lesson on academic writing for first-year undergraduate students studying through ODL. The lesson should include an introduction, measurable learning outcomes, learner-friendly explanations, worked examples, learner activities, self-assessment questions, and a summary.

In contextual prompting, the learners and the learning setting are described before content is requested. It should not be assumed that the AI is aware of the target audience. The prompt should state the learners’ prior knowledge, the course level, the expected duration, and any institutional requirements. The more specific the description, the less revision is usually required.

Prompt
Prepare a lesson on research methods for first-year undergraduate students studying through ODL. Assume that learners have completed secondary education but have no previous knowledge of research methods. Explain concepts using simple language, practical examples, short paragraphs, and frequent opportunities for learner reflection.

In few-shot prompting, the AI is given one or two examples of the required output instead of an abstract description. This technique is particularly useful when several academics contribute to the same course and need to follow an existing style.

Prompt
The following lesson illustrates the structure used throughout this course. Analyse its organisation and writing style, then develop a new lesson on sustainable development using the same structure, level of detail, and writing style.

In iterative prompting, the lesson is developed through a series of smaller prompts instead of a single large request, and it is refined and expanded at each stage. A typical sequence is as follows:

  • Step 1: Generate the lesson outline.
  • Step 2: Expand each lesson section.
  • Step 3: Develop worked examples.
  • Step 4: Generate learner activities.
  • Step 5: Create formative assessment questions.
  • Step 6: Write the lesson summary.
  • Step 7: Review the lesson for clarity and consistency.

Prompt chaining extends iterative prompting by using the output of one prompt as the input for the next. The outline becomes the basis for the detailed explanations, which in turn form the basis for the examples, activities, and assessments. This reflects the way a course is developed manually, and it usually produces more coherent material than a single request.

Prompt engineering activity

Select one lesson that you are preparing and develop it using each technique in turn: first a simple prompt, then role, contextual, few-shot, and iterative prompting. Compare the outputs and reflect on which technique produced the most useful results.

Good practice

Effective prompt engineering seldom involves a single interaction. A prompt usually needs to be refined several times before the output is suitable for inclusion in course materials.

Table 7.1
Selecting Prompting Techniques for Different Course Development Tasks
Course Development TaskRecommended TechniqueWhy It Is Effective
Planning a lessonContextual PromptingGenerates an organised lesson structure aligned with learner needs.
Writing learning outcomesRole PromptingProduces measurable outcomes using an instructional design perspective.
Developing lesson contentContextual + IterativeSupports learner-centred explanations that can be refined progressively.
Creating worked examplesRole PromptingProduces discipline-specific examples appropriate for the intended audience.
Developing learner activitiesContextual PromptingAligns activities with learning outcomes and learner characteristics.
Creating self-assessment questionsIterative PromptingEnables progressive improvement of question quality and feedback.
Revising existing materialsFew-Shot PromptingMaintains consistency with the style and structure of existing course materials.
Preparing PowerPoint presentationsPrompt ChainingConverts lesson content into structured presentation slides.
Developing Moodle quizzesPrompt ChainingGenerates questions, answers, feedback, and question banks systematically.
Note. Recommendations reflect typical use across the techniques introduced earlier in this chapter. A given task may still benefit from a different technique depending on the subject and the learner group.

7.9 Choosing the Right AI Tool

Generative AI tools may appear similar, but they differ in their strengths. Some are suited to developing lesson content, while others specialise in presentations, diagrams, document analysis, or research. No single tool is suitable for every task, and a combination of complementary tools usually produces better results.

Practical activity

Select one lesson and identify three tools that could support it: one for content, one for activities and assessments, and one for a visual resource. Compare the outputs and reflect on which combination best suits your workflow.

Good practice

Tools should be selected according to the requirements of the task rather than their popularity. Irrespective of the tool used, every generated resource must be reviewed for accuracy, pedagogical suitability, and alignment with the learning outcomes before publication.

Quality Assurance

Generative AI can reduce drafting time considerably; however, responsibility for academic quality remains with the academic at every stage described in this chapter. Research on AI in higher education has given limited attention to the role of the educator (Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019). For this reason, the review process described below is essential.

Figure 7.9
The Draft, Review, Revise, Approve Cycle
Note. Every AI-assisted lesson passes through this loop before it reaches a learner. A draft that fails review returns for revision rather than moving forward to approval.

All AI-generated content should be treated as a draft that requires review. The academic should check its technical accuracy, confirm that it is aligned with the learning outcomes and that the examples are appropriate, and revise the language where necessary to maintain consistency across the course.

Generative AI supports the writing process, but authorship and accountability remain with the academic. Effective course materials combine an AI-generated draft with the academic’s subject expertise, teaching experience, and understanding of the learners. The materials are then reviewed for accuracy, consistency, accessibility, and compliance with institutional standards before they are released to learners.

The UNESCO guidance on generative AI in education may be used as a reference point, and the use of AI in developing each lesson should be recorded so that the course team can review it (Chan, 2023; Cotton et al., 2024; Miao & Holmes, 2023). Learner data, unpublished institutional material, and copyrighted content should not be entered into public AI tools without permission. Generated text and images should be checked for bias, and the licence terms of any AI-generated image should be confirmed before use.

AI systems can produce errors, such as inaccurate information, missing concepts, or examples that do not suit the learning context (Ji et al., 2023). References require particular care, since AI tools can generate citations that appear authentic but do not exist (Walters & Wilder, 2023). Every AI-generated output should therefore be read critically before it becomes part of the official course material.

Quality checklist
  • Have all facts, figures, and technical claims been verified against a trusted source?
  • Do the learning outcomes, explanations, examples, and assessment items align with one another?
  • Are the examples and case studies appropriate for the intended learners, and localised where relevant?
  • Has every reference or citation produced by the AI been checked, since these can be fabricated?
  • Does the language, tone, and level of detail match the rest of the course material?
  • Has the content been reviewed against institutional quality standards before publication?
Figure 7.10
Quality Assurance Checkpoints Before Publication
Note. These six checkpoints summarise the quality checklist above in a form suited to a final check before a lesson is published.

Chapter Seven · Page 7 of 9

Reflection, Summary, Resources & References

Reflection

Consider the following questions as you reflect on integrating generative AI into your own practice.

  • Which stages of your current course development process take the most time, and could generative AI reasonably support them?
  • Which aspects of writing a lesson would you not delegate to AI, and why?
  • How will you build a review step into your workflow, so every AI-generated draft is checked before it reaches a learner?
  • Which prompting technique is most suited to your own style of writing?
  • How might you adapt AI-generated examples so they reflect the Sri Lankan and OUSL context for your learners?

Summary

Generative AI has become a useful resource for developing ODL course materials. When used appropriately, it can assist academics in planning lessons, writing learner-centred explanations, developing worked examples and case studies, designing activities, preparing formative assessments, improving the clarity of written text, and creating supporting multimedia resources. Effective prompt engineering produces more relevant output, and the selection of an appropriate tool for each stage saves time.

Responsibility for academic quality, however, remains with the academic. When generative AI is combined with sound instructional design and professional judgement, it can support the development of learner-centred course materials for independent learning.

Appendix A: Prompt Templates

These templates can be copied and adapted by replacing the text in square brackets. Select a template to view it.

Prompt
You are an experienced instructional designer at the OUSL. Develop a lesson outline for the course [Course Name] on the topic [Topic]. The lesson is intended for [learner level] studying through ODL. Include: lesson title; introduction; learning outcomes; prerequisite knowledge; main lesson sections; suggested examples; learner activities; self-assessment questions; lesson summary. Write using clear academic language suitable for independent learners.
Prompt
Explain the topic [Topic] for [learner level] students studying independently through ODL. Use: simple academic language; short paragraphs; headings and subheadings; practical examples; analogies where appropriate; reflection questions throughout; a summary at the end.
Prompt
Generate three worked examples for the topic [Topic]. Each example should: explain the problem; solve it step by step; explain the reasoning; identify common mistakes; conclude with a short learner exercise.
Prompt
Develop learner-centred activities for the lesson [Topic]. Include: one reflection activity; one practical activity; one case study; one discussion activity; one collaborative activity suitable for Moodle. Align all activities with the learning outcomes.
Prompt
Develop formative assessment questions for the lesson [Topic]. Include: five multiple-choice questions; three short-answer questions; one scenario-based question; model answers; explanations for every answer.
Prompt
Review the following lesson as an instructional designer. Evaluate: accuracy; organisation; clarity; readability; learner engagement; alignment with learning outcomes; opportunities for learner interaction. Suggest improvements without changing the academic meaning.
Prompt
Rewrite the following lesson section for undergraduate students studying independently through ODL. Improve: clarity; readability; logical flow; transitions; consistency. Maintain academic accuracy and preserve the original meaning.
Prompt
Based on the following lesson, recommend Moodle learning activities that would support learner engagement. Suggest appropriate uses of: Forum; Quiz; Assignment; H5P Interactive Content; Lesson Activity; Glossary; Database Activity; Workshop. Explain how each supports the intended learning outcomes.
Prompt
Convert the following lesson into a presentation for an Interactive Learning Session (ILS). Produce: slide titles; concise bullet points; speaker notes; suggested diagrams; learner questions; summary slide. The presentation should support learner participation during the ILS.
Prompt
Develop an assessment rubric for the following assignment. Include: assessment criteria; performance levels; marks allocation; descriptors for Excellent, Good, Satisfactory and Needs Improvement. Ensure alignment with the learning outcomes.
Prompt
Suggest visual learning resources for the lesson [Topic]. Recommend: concept maps; flowcharts; diagrams; infographics; timelines; comparison tables. For each, explain how it supports learner understanding.
Prompt
Adapt the following lesson for learners studying in Sri Lanka. Replace generic international examples with examples from: Sri Lankan education; government organisations; healthcare; agriculture; engineering; banking; business. Ensure the examples remain culturally appropriate and educationally relevant.

Closing

Conclusion

This guidebook began with an introduction to multimodal instructional materials in Open and Distance Learning. It then discussed the modes through which materials reach learners, and the development of print-based materials, audio-visual resources and LMS-based courses. It concludes with the use of generative AI to support, but not replace, the work of the academic.

Although the seven chapters were written by several contributors, they share a common set of principles: materials should be designed around the needs of the learner, learning outcomes should guide each design decision, and the academic remains responsible for the final content.

The guidebook is intended as a working reference. Its tables, templates, activities and checklists may be consulted whenever a session is planned or revised.

Practices in distance education continue to change, and this guidebook will be revised accordingly. Suggestions for improvement may be forwarded to CETMe for consideration in the next edition.
